Bulk graphite · SWMcC model · density of states

ERS background of bulk graphite

Density of states of pure hexagonal (AB) and rhombohedral (ABC) bulk graphite, as an estimate of the electronic Raman scattering (ERS) continuum of the two polytypes within the 80–6200 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) range of the spectrometer.

0.04 → 1.05rhombohedral / hexagonal DOS from 80 to 6200 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)
5020Raman shift in \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) at which the two DOS curves cross
5–384 meV\(|E - E_F|\) probed by the spectrometer, \(\hbar\omega/2\)
0.007rhombohedral / hexagonal DOS at the Fermi level

From the ERS signal to the density of states

In graphene, few-layer graphene and graphite the ERS continuum consists of interband electron–hole excitations with negligible momentum transfer. They are created through a virtual intermediate state, appear in crossed polarisation (\(A_{2g}\) symmetry), and the matrix element is nearly independent of energy (Kashuba and Fal'ko 2009; Ponosov et al. 2015). Ponosov et al. model the spectrum of bulk graphite with a constant matrix element. In the limit of small damping their Eq. (1) reads

\[I(\omega) \propto \frac{1}{1 - e^{-\hbar\omega/k_B T}} \sum_{c,v} \int d^3p\,\left[f(\varepsilon_v) - f(\varepsilon_c)\right]\delta\!\left(\hbar\omega - \varepsilon_c(\mathbf{p}) + \varepsilon_v(\mathbf{p})\right).\]

García-Ruiz et al. (2019), Eq. (5), find that the Raman vertex is proportional to \((\mathbf{l} \times \mathbf{l}')_z\,\sigma_z\), so the excitations that count connect each valence band to its mirror conduction band, \(n^- \to n^+\), and the spectral density reflects the joint density of states of electrons and holes. For bands that are mirror images about the Fermi level, \(\varepsilon_c = -\varepsilon_v\), the joint density of states at \(\hbar\omega\) is half the density of states at \(\hbar\omega/2\). This gives the working rule of this report:

\[I_\mathrm{ERS}(\omega) \propto D\!\left(E_F \pm \frac{\hbar\omega}{2}\right).\]

A Raman shift \(\omega\) therefore reads the DOS at an energy \(\hbar\omega/2\) from the Fermi level, and 80–6200 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) (9.9–769 meV) corresponds to \(|E - E_F|\) = 5.0–384 meV. The same reading underlies the layer-number assignment of Pálinkás et al. (2024), where the ERS peaks of rhombohedral films sit at the separation of the \(-n\) and \(+n\) DOS peaks.

Model

Both crystals are described by the Slonczewski–Weiss–McClure tight-binding model of this repository (multilayer_graphene.py, parameters of McEllistrim et al. 2023) extended to an infinite stack (bulk_graphite.py): every hop from layer \(n\) to layer \(n + m\) carries the phase \(e^{i m k_z d}\), \(d = 3.35\) Å. The two polytypes use the same couplings and have the same atomic density, \(1.139\times10^{23}\) \(\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\), so their DOS can be compared per atom or per volume.

Couplings, identical for the two polytypes
couplingvalue (eV)role
\(\gamma_0\)3.0896intralayer nearest neighbour (\(v = 1.0\times10^{6}\) m/s)
\(\gamma_1\)0.390vertical dimer coupling
\(\gamma_2\)−0.017next-nearest layer, through a hexagon centre
\(\gamma_3\)0.3090skew, non-dimer sites (trigonal warping)
\(\gamma_4\)0.0680skew, dimer to non-dimer (electron–hole asymmetry)
\(\gamma_5\)0.038next-nearest layer, along a dimer chain
\(\Delta'\)0.025on-site energy per \(\gamma_1\) bond
  • Hexagonal graphite. Two layers per cell. On the K–H line the model gives the SWMcC energies\[E_{1,2} = 2\Delta' - \gamma_5 + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma_5\Gamma^2 \pm \gamma_1\Gamma, \qquad E_3 = -\gamma_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\gamma_2\Gamma^2, \qquad \Gamma = 2\cos(k_z d),\]that is the standard model with \(\Delta = 2\Delta' + \gamma_2 - \gamma_5 = -5\) meV. At each \(k_z\) the bands are those of a bilayer with coupling \(\gamma_1\Gamma\), which leaves a finite DOS at the Fermi level.
  • Rhombohedral graphite. One layer per primitive cell, every atom has one \(\gamma_1\) bond. The bands are Dirac cones whose apex moves on a spiral of radius \(\gamma_1/\hbar v\) around the K–H line (McClure 1969). To first order in the small couplings the apex energy is\[E_D(k_z) \simeq \Delta' + \frac{2\gamma_1\gamma_4}{\gamma_0} + \frac{2\gamma_4}{\gamma_0}\left(\frac{\gamma_1\gamma_3}{\gamma_0} + \frac{\gamma_2}{2}\right)\cos(3k_z d),\]a mean of 42.2 meV and a total width of 2.7 meV, which is the band overlap of the semimetal.

Density of states of the two polytypes

Fermi-level quantities from charge neutrality
hexagonal (AB)rhombohedral (ABC)
Fermi level on the model's energy scale (meV)−2.7+42.3
electrons = holes at \(T = 0\) (\(\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\))\(2.0\times10^{18}\)\(1.2\times10^{15}\)
DOS at the Fermi level (states \(\mathrm{eV^{-1}\,atom^{-1}}\))\(4.9\times10^{-3}\)\(3.6\times10^{-5}\)
  • Hexagonal graphite has a finite DOS at the Fermi level and a slow, nearly linear rise on both sides. The structure within about 25 meV of \(E_F\) comes from the low-energy bands along K–H, whose energy varies by \(2|\gamma_2|\) between K and H and which \(\gamma_3\) warps trigonally; the kinks near \(-0.69\) and \(+0.87\) eV are the edges of the split bands at K (\(\pm 2\gamma_1\)).
  • Rhombohedral graphite has the linear DOS of graphene, per layer, and it vanishes at the Fermi level to within the 2.7 meV band overlap.
  • The hole side of hexagonal graphite carries 25–40 % more states than the electron side (\(\gamma_4\) and \(\Delta'\)), while rhombohedral graphite is symmetric to 0.2 %. The two curves therefore cross at \(+0.21\) eV for electrons and do not cross for holes within 1 eV.

  • Across the window the hexagonal DOS grows by a factor of 3.0, the rhombohedral DOS by a factor of 78.

What the estimate leaves out

  • Thermal factors. For mirror bands the occupation factor of Eq. (1) is \(\tanh(\hbar\omega/4k_B T)\), and the Stokes prefactor is \(\left[1 - e^{-\hbar\omega/k_B T}\right]^{-1}\). Their product rises from \(1/4\) at \(\omega \to 0\) to 1 above roughly \(\hbar\omega = 8k_B T\) (1700 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) at 300 K). It multiplies both polytypes alike, so the ratios above are unaffected.
  • Spectral shape at large shifts. Ponosov et al. measure a broad maximum near 3000 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) in graphite and in graphene, where the joint density of states keeps rising, and discuss a phonon-assisted channel as a possible reason. The DOS is a safer guide to the ratio of the two polytypes than to the absolute line shape.
  • Mirror symmetry. The rule \(D(E_F \pm \hbar\omega/2)\) assumes \(\varepsilon_c = -\varepsilon_v\). The table averages the electron and hole sides, which differ by 25–40 % in hexagonal graphite inside the window.
  • Fermi surface of hexagonal graphite. Electron and hole pockets block the excitations below a few tens of meV at low temperature; at room temperature Ponosov et al. find no gap down to 50 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\).
  • Surfaces and stacking faults. Figures 1 and 2 are the bulk DOS. Finite rhombohedral films add the surface flat band and the subband edges that produce the ERS peaks of Pálinkás et al. (2024), shown for thick slabs below; stacking faults add their own features.
  • Parameters. McClure (1969), with \(|\gamma_4| \approx 0.25\)–\(0.28\) eV and further next-nearest-plane couplings, estimated a band overlap of 14–26 meV for rhombohedral graphite and a Fermi-level DOS of 0.07 of the hexagonal value. With the present couplings (\(\gamma_4 = 0.068\) eV) the overlap is 2.7 meV and the ratio 0.007. The difference is confined to \(|E - E_F|\) of the order of the overlap, below the 5 meV where the window starts.

Numerical details and checks

  • \(k_z\) is sampled at 240 values over half of its period. For each value the in-plane integral uses linear interpolation on triangles of a square mesh around K (spacing 0.002 \(\text{Å}^{-1}\)). Cells in which a band comes within 0.12 eV of the Fermi level are subdivided 8 times (hexagonal) or 32 times (rhombohedral). Energy bins are 1 meV wide, with no further smoothing.
  • With these default settings, halving the mesh spacing, doubling the number of \(k_z\) values or doubling the subdivision changes the hexagonal DOS by at most 0.1 % at all energies. The rhombohedral DOS changes by less than 0.1 % for \(|E - E_F| > 3\) meV and by 0.7 % inside.
  • The Fermi level follows from charge neutrality at \(T = 0\). The carrier density of hexagonal graphite, \(2.0\times10^{18}\) \(\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\) of each sign, compares with the \(25\times10^{-6}\) carriers per atom (\(2.8\times10^{18}\) \(\mathrm{cm^{-3}}\)) that McClure (1969) quotes for hexagonal graphite.
  • Tests (tests/test_bulk_graphite.py): the K–H energies of hexagonal graphite equal the SWMcC expressions; bulk Bloch states solve the finite-stack Hamiltonian of multilayer_graphene.py in its interior to \(10^{-12}\) eV; with \(\gamma_0\) and \(\gamma_1\) only, the rhombohedral DOS equals that of graphene and the hexagonal DOS equals the \(k_z\) average of bilayers.

Reproduce

python -m pytest tests -q
python graphite_ers_background.py --raman-min 80 --raman-max 6200 --slabs 20 50 100
python graphite_ers_background.py --from-csv examples/graphite_ers_dos.csv --raman-min 50   # replot only

Finite slabs: 20, 50 and 100 layers

The same tight-binding model for slabs of \(N\) layers with free surfaces (multilayer_graphene.py, \(2N\) bands), hexagonal (ABAB…) and rhombohedral (ABCABC…). The DOS is divided by the \(2N\) atoms of the cell, so it can be laid over the bulk curves, and each slab has its own Fermi level from charge neutrality.

Fermi level on the model's energy scale, and DOS averaged over \(|E - E_F|\) = 5–384 meV (both signs) in \(10^{-2}\) states \(\mathrm{eV^{-1}\,atom^{-1}}\)
\(E_F\) hexagonal (meV)\(E_F\) rhombohedral (meV)hexagonalrhombohedralrhombohedral / hexagonal
20 layers−2.6+19.00.9220.7560.820
50 layers−2.7+22.40.9290.7630.821
100 layers−2.7+23.70.9310.7640.821
bulk−2.7+42.30.9330.7650.819
  • Hexagonal slabs follow the bulk curve. Between 30 meV and the upper edge of the window the largest deviation is 3.5 %, 1.3 % and 0.7 % for 20, 50 and 100 layers. The discrete subbands show only as small steps within about 20 meV of the Fermi level.
  • Rhombohedral slabs resolve the bulk continuum into a ladder of subbands. Each subband starts with a step and a van Hove peak. The \(-n\) and \(+n\) peaks pair into the ERS peaks of García-Ruiz et al. (2019),\[\hbar\omega_n \approx 4\gamma_1 \sin\!\left[\frac{\left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)\pi}{2N + 1}\right].\]The first one lies at 1443, 587 and 295 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) for 20, 50 and 100 layers, and the peaks follow each other every \(4\pi\gamma_1/(2N + 1) =\) 964, 391 and 197 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\). In the 20-layer DOS the first two pairs of peaks are 177 and 294 meV apart; the formula gives 179 and 297 meV.
  • Thick rhombohedral slabs give a bulk-like background. The measured ERS peaks of thin films are about 500 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) wide at room temperature (Pálinkás et al. 2024). The ladders of the 50- and 100-layer slabs are finer than that and merge into a continuum that follows the envelope of the DOS, and that envelope is the bulk curve: averaged between 30 meV and the upper edge of the window the slab DOS is 95.7 %, 98.2 % and 99.1 % of the bulk DOS for 20, 50 and 100 layers.
  • Surface band. The plateau about 30 meV wide at the Fermi level of the rhombohedral slabs is the surface band. It holds \(2(\gamma_1/\hbar v)^2 A_\mathrm{cell}/\pi =\) 0.012 states per unit cell of the film (two surfaces, spin and valley included) whatever the thickness, so its height per atom falls as \(1/N\).
  • Fermi level of the rhombohedral slabs. The surface band pins the Fermi level 23, 20 and 19 meV below the bulk Dirac energy for 20, 50 and 100 layers. The dashed bulk curves are drawn at the same absolute energy, which puts their minimum to the right of zero. The \(n^- \to n^+\) pairs are centred near the Dirac energy and not on \(E_F\), so for the subbands the shaded window should be read as shifted by that amount. At low temperature the pairs with \(\hbar\omega/2\) smaller than the offset (shifts below about 300 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\)) are Pauli blocked. The offset belongs to the non-interacting model, which leaves out the charge redistribution between surface and interior.

Numerical details: in-plane mesh around K with spacing 0.001 \(\text{Å}^{-1}\) and half-width 0.18 \(\text{Å}^{-1}\), triangle interpolation, 1 meV bins, no smoothing. Only \(p_y \ge 0\) is diagonalised; the other half follows from \(E(p_x, -p_y) = E(p_x, p_y)\). For 20 layers, halving the mesh spacing changes single 1 meV bins at subband edges by up to \(0.04\times10^{-2}\) states \(\mathrm{eV^{-1}\,atom^{-1}}\) and the rest of the curves by less; the thicker slabs were not repeated on a finer mesh.

Thermal broadening at 300 K

The same curves with the energy scale smeared at \(T = 300\) K: each DOS is convolved with the derivative of the Fermi function,

\[D_T(E) = \int D(E')\left(-\frac{\partial f}{\partial E}\right)_{E - E'} dE', \qquad -\frac{\partial f}{\partial E} = \frac{1}{4k_B T}\,\operatorname{sech}^2\!\left(\frac{E}{2k_B T}\right),\]

with \(k_B T = 25.9\) meV. The kernel has a full width at half maximum of \(3.53\,k_B T = 91\) meV on the energy axis, which is \(7.05\,k_B T\) or 1470 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) on the Raman-shift axis \(\hbar\omega = 2|E - E_F|\).

  • Bulk. The broadening fills the minimum of the rhombohedral DOS: at the Fermi level it is 0.14 against 0.55 for hexagonal graphite (\(10^{-2}\) states \(\mathrm{eV^{-1}\,atom^{-1}}\)). At 80 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) the ratio of the two is 0.26, against 0.04 without broadening. From 2000 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) upwards the broadening changes the ratio by less than 0.01, and the curves cross at 5070 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\).
  • The subband ladders are gone. No step or van Hove peak of the slabs survives the broadening. The hexagonal slabs stay within 2.6 %, 1.0 % and 0.5 % of the bulk curve for 20, 50 and 100 layers over the whole window.
  • What remains of the film is its surface band. The rhombohedral slabs carry extra states at the Fermi level: 0.36, 0.24 and 0.19 for 20, 50 and 100 layers against 0.14 in the bulk, which is 124 %, 51 % and 26 % above the bulk curve at the same absolute energy. The excess scales as \(1/N\) and sits at the low end of the window: at 80 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) the ratio to the hexagonal DOS is 0.66, 0.43 and 0.35 against 0.26 in the bulk, while from 2000 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) upwards the slab ratios are within 7 % of the bulk ratio.
  • How to read this for ERS. In Eq. (1) temperature enters through the occupation factors, not as a convolution of the DOS, so these curves show how much structure a thermal smearing of the energy scale leaves, not the ERS line shape. On the Raman-shift axis the kernel is 1470 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) wide, about 3 times the 500 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) width of the ERS peaks that Pálinkás et al. (2024) measure at room temperature, so the figure overstates the smearing of ERS features. --temperature sets the kernel; 102 K gives a width of 500 \(\mathrm{cm^{-1}}\) on the Raman-shift axis.

Numerical details: the kernel is integrated over each energy bin. The slab curves end at \(|E - E_F| = 0.5\) eV and are continued by the bulk curve at the same absolute energy before the convolution; at the upper edge of the window 1.1 % of the kernel weight falls on that continuation.
